newsitem.title: USA: U.S. allows aid flight to go to Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. allows aid flight to go to Cuba.

text.p: The U.S. government has waived a ban on direct flights from the United States to Cuba to let a Roman Catholic Church charity send a planeload of aid for victims of Hurricane Lili, the State Department said on Wednesday.

Spokesman Nicholas Burns said the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control had approved an application from Catholic Relief Services to charter an emergency humanitarian flight to deliver supplies to Cuba.
Burns' comment confirmed a statement in Havana on Tuesday by the Cuban Catholic organisation Caritas Cubana.
Caritas director Rolando Suarez said the plane would probably fly from Miami to the central city of Cienfuegos on Wednesday or Thursday with some 78 tonnes of food aid.
Suarez said it would be the first aid to arrive following an international appeal on Monday by Caritas Cubana.

Hurricane Lili swept the central and western areas of Cuba last Thursday and Friday. It destroyed more than 5,000 homes and damaged 78,000 and caused extensive damage to crops, power lines and communications.

The aid plane will be a rare direct flight from the United States since President Bill Clinton banned charter flights to and from the island after Cuba shot down two small private U.S. planes on Feb. 24. Cuban athletes were allowed to fly directly to and from Atlanta in July for the Olympic Games.
"It's important, we thought, to allow a non-governmental organisation to be able to reach out and provide this type of assistance directly to the Cuban people," Burns told a news briefing.

Burns and other officials described the waiver as consistent with America's Cuban Democracy Act and Helms-Burton Act which enforce sanctions against the communist-ruled island but encourage people-to-people contacts.

"Here is a very good example, in the wake of tragedy where a lot of Cubans are suffering, where an American organisation can make a difference through the provision of humanitarian assistance," Burns said.

"Despite the fact that we have a very difficult political relationship with (President Fidel) Castro's government, that we're an opponent of his government, there are times when the American people need to connect with the Cuban people."

Another official said that since the Cuban Democracy Act was passed in 1992, the United States had sent about $140 million in aid to private groups in Cuba -- more than all private donations to Cuba from the rest of the world combined.
"The issue is how we ensure we are not giving aid to the Cuban government," said the official.

Cuban Americans, mostly in Florida, have mobilised to send aid to Cuba, but some say no aid should be sent to the island. They argue that such help might not reach victims of the storm but would be used by the Havana government.
